pedagogy.summary: At 9-11 the star life cycle is a story with a BRANCH decided by one variable — mass. All stars are born in clouds of gas and dust (nebulae/molecular clouds) that gravity pulls together until the core gets hot and dense enough to FUSE hydrogen into helium; this fusion is what makes a star shine, for millions to billions of years (the long, stable 'main sequence' — where our Sun is now). When the core's hydrogen runs low the star swells and then dies — and HOW it dies depends on how massive it was: lower-mass, Sun-like stars gently puff off their outer layers and leave a small, cooling core called a WHITE DWARF, while very massive stars end in a colossal SUPERNOVA explosion. The two big ideas are (1) the born→shine→die sequence powered by hydrogen fusion, and (2) mass decides the ending.
bestPractices: Tell it as a life story with named stages — nebula → (protostar) → main-sequence star fusing hydrogen → swelling giant → white dwarf OR supernova — so the sequence has a clear shape the child can retell.

Make MASS the pivot and teach the branch explicitly: same beginning for all stars, but massive stars live fast and die in a supernova, while smaller stars live long and fade to a white dwarf — 'how big it is decides how it ends'.
Anchor 'why stars shine' in fusion at an age-appropriate level: the core squeezes hydrogen together to make helium and releases energy — no need for equations, but name fusion as the engine.

Use real imagery (nebulae like Orion, a supernova remnant, the Sun as a main-sequence star) to keep the abstract timescales tangible and awe-driven; connect to prior learning that the Sun is an ordinary main-sequence star.

Handle the enormous timescales carefully: stars live millions-to-billions of years, so we never watch one star change — we see many stars at different stages, like photographing a forest to infer a tree's life.
keyRepresentations: Life-cycle flow with a branch: nebula → main-sequence star → [low mass → giant → white dwarf] / [high mass → supergiant → supernova]
A MASS dial/scale that sends the same starting star down the small-star or big-star path
Nebula ('star nursery') image where gravity clumps gas into a new star
Side-by-side endings: gentle planetary-nebula + white dwarf vs violent supernova
The Sun marked as 'here, now' on the main sequence, roughly halfway through its life
commonMisconceptions: Thinking all stars end the same way — not realising a star's MASS decides whether it becomes a white dwarf or explodes as a supernova.
Believing stars are 'on fire'/burning like a bonfire, rather than shining by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium.
Thinking we can watch a single star go through its life — missing that the stages take millions/billions of years and we infer the cycle from many stars at different stages.
Assuming bigger stars live longer (they actually burn out far faster) — confusing size with lifespan.
Thinking a star's death is a total disappearance, not realising it leaves a remnant (white dwarf, or after a supernova a dense core) and scatters material that seeds new stars.
Confusing a nebula (gas-and-dust cloud where stars form) with a galaxy (a vast collection of stars).

learn.summary: Teach the star life cycle (ages 9-11) as a story with one branch point decided by MASS: all stars are born in clouds of gas and dust (nebulae) that gravity pulls together until the core is hot and dense enough to fuse hydrogen into helium — which is what makes a star shine for millions to billions of years on the stable main sequence. When core hydrogen runs low the star swells and dies, and HOW it dies depends on mass: lower-mass Sun-like stars swell to a giant, puff off their outer layers and leave a cooling white dwarf, while very massive stars swell to a supergiant and end in a supernova. Two big ideas: the born→shine→die sequence powered by fusion, and mass deciding the ending (including the surprising twist that bigger stars live SHORTER lives). A mass-controlled interactive may be a particularly direct way for a learner to discover mass→fate; a labelled branching diagram, awe imagery, and a sequencing check are valuable alternatives serving different purposes.

activities.title: Set the mass, watch the fate
feedback: If a learner expects the big star to last longest, point to the two lifespan counters: the massive star's ran out first — more fuel but burned far faster and hotter, lasting only a few million years versus billions for a small star.

If a learner thinks the Sun will explode, replay the low-mass/Sun path: it swells into a giant, then sheds a ring and leaves a white dwarf — no supernova; supernovae are reserved for much more massive stars.

If a learner calls the shining 'fire', note the star shines by fusion (joining hydrogen into helium in the core), not by burning like a bonfire; ordinary burning could never release enough energy to keep a star shining for millions or billions of years.
Reinforce the click-moment: 'Same birth — the mass you set decided the ending.'
activities.rationale: The concept is a process with a single-variable branch, so letting the learner set mass and watch the fate follow is intended to turn 'mass decides fate' from a told fact into a discovered one; the lifespan readout directly confronts the 'bigger lives longer' misconception.
sourceClaims: Stars form in large clouds of gas and dust (molecular clouds/nebulae) that collapse under gravity into protostars; main-sequence stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores, which releases energy that balances gravity; the Sun is a main-sequence star about midway through its life.

The details of a star's death depend strongly on its MASS: lower-mass, Sun-like stars shed their outer layers as a planetary nebula and leave a white dwarf, while massive stars end in a supernova (leaving a dense remnant); more massive stars burn their fuel far faster and live much shorter lives.
learnerActions: Start with a glowing cloud of gas and dust (a nebula) on screen and a single MASS dial/slider as the control.

Set the mass LOW and press play: watch the cloud collapse, a star ignite (hydrogen fusing into helium), shine steadily for a very long time, then swell into a giant and gently puff off a glowing ring, leaving a tiny white ember (white dwarf).
Rewind, crank the mass dial HIGH, and press play again: watch the star blaze through its life startlingly fast, swell into a supergiant, and end in a blinding supernova.
Read a lifespan counter each run so the 'live fast, die young' contrast is concrete — the massive star's counter runs out far sooner.
Try a 'Sun' preset that drops a marker on the main sequence 'here, now', roughly halfway along the gentle low-mass path.
Say in your own words what stayed the same across both runs and what changed.
activities.intendedInsight: It is the SAME kind of birth for every star; how massive the star is decides how it dies — and the biggest stars die youngest, not oldest.

activities.title: Walk the branching life-cycle diagram
feedback: If a learner stumbles on the order, have them re-tap the stages from nebula to ending before retelling.
If a learner forgets the branch, point back to the labelled fork: small star → giant → white dwarf, massive star → supergiant → supernova.
Confirm the Sun sits on the gentle low-mass path heading to white dwarf, not supernova.
activities.rationale: A labelled branching diagram with tap-to-reveal facts reliably teaches the sequence and the two endings and supports retelling; it depicts the branch clearly even though it does not let the learner set the mass and watch the fate follow, so it complements rather than replaces the interactive.
sourceClaims: The details of a star's death depend strongly on its MASS: lower-mass, Sun-like stars shed their outer layers as a planetary nebula and leave a white dwarf, while massive stars end in a supernova (leaving a dense remnant); more massive stars burn their fuel far faster and live much shorter lives.
learnerActions: Follow a labelled life-cycle flow with the fork at the main-sequence stage: nebula → main-sequence star, then branching to [low mass → giant → white dwarf] OR [high mass → supergiant → supernova].
Tap each stage to reveal what is happening there (gravity clumps gas; the core fuses hydrogen into helium; the star swells; the ending).
Use the clearly labelled fork marked 'small star' vs 'massive star' to state which ending each path leads to and why.
Open the flap on the Sun to read 'a main-sequence star, about halfway through its life'.
Retell the whole sequence from memory, naming each stage including the giant or supergiant step.
activities.intendedInsight: The life cycle has a clear, retellable shape with named stages, and the ending forks on whether the star is small (giant → white dwarf) or massive (supergiant → supernova).

activities.title: Awe imagery of birth and death
feedback: If a learner expects to watch a single star age, remind them each stage lasts millions to billions of years; astronomers piece the cycle together from many stars at different stages.
If a learner confuses a nebula with a galaxy, clarify: a nebula is a cloud of gas and dust where stars form; a galaxy is a vast collection of stars.
Link the Sun image to prior learning that it is an ordinary main-sequence star.
activities.rationale: Spectacular imagery builds engagement and anchors the enormous timescales, and the 'many stars at different stages' framing addresses the misconception that we observe one star's whole life; this supports wonder and timescale understanding rather than the causal mass→fate move.
sourceClaims: Stars form in large clouds of gas and dust (molecular clouds/nebulae) that collapse under gravity into protostars; main-sequence stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores, which releases energy that balances gravity; the Sun is a main-sequence star about midway through its life.
learnerActions: View real imagery of a star nursery nebula (e.g. the Orion Nebula), the Sun as an ordinary main-sequence star, and a supernova remnant.
Optionally take a fly-through of a nebula or a supernova set-piece as a wonder moment.
Match each image to its place on the life-cycle story you learned.
Discuss why we never watch one star change: stages take millions to billions of years, so we see many stars at different stages — like photographing a forest to infer one tree's life.
activities.intendedInsight: The abstract timescales become tangible and awe-inspiring through real images, and we infer the cycle from many stars caught at different stages rather than watching one.

activities.title: Check the sequence and the branch
feedback: If a learner orders the stages wrongly, replay the diagram walkthrough and retry.
If a learner picks 'size/brightness' over mass, restate that mass is the property that decides both lifespan and ending.
If a learner says the massive star lasts longer, explain it burns its larger fuel supply far faster and hotter, so it lasts only a few million years while the Sun shines for billions.
activities.rationale: A short sequencing-and-matching check verifies the stage order and the mass branch after teaching; it confirms recall but does not itself build the causal 'mass decides fate' intuition, so it belongs after the interactive or diagram work.
sourceClaims: The details of a star's death depend strongly on its MASS: lower-mass, Sun-like stars shed their outer layers as a planetary nebula and leave a white dwarf, while massive stars end in a supernova (leaving a dense remnant); more massive stars burn their fuel far faster and live much shorter lives.
learnerActions: Put the life stages in order with the branch intact: nebula → main-sequence star → then either (low mass) giant → white dwarf, or (high mass) supergiant → supernova.
Answer: 'What single property decides whether a star becomes a white dwarf or a supernova?' (its mass).
Match each mass (small / massive) to its ending (white dwarf / supernova).
Answer the surprise puzzle: which lasts longer, a huge massive star or a small one like the Sun — and why?
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can recall and apply the stage order and its branch, name mass as the deciding property, and recognise that massive stars live shortest.

constraints: Keep fusion age-appropriate: name it as the core squeezing hydrogen together to make helium and releasing energy; no equations required.
Emphasise that mass decides BOTH how a star lives (lifespan) and how it dies — and surface the counter-intuitive twist that more massive stars burn out far faster, so they live shorter lives.

The Sun will NOT supernova: it becomes a red giant then sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf; reserve supernovae for much more massive stars (which swell to supergiants first).
Keep the two swollen stages distinct: low-mass stars become giants before the white dwarf; massive stars become supergiants before the supernova.
Address the timescale honestly: stars live millions to billions of years, so we never watch one star change — we infer the cycle from many stars at different stages.
Distinguish a nebula (gas-and-dust cloud where stars form) from a galaxy (a vast collection of stars).
Note that a star's death leaves a remnant (white dwarf, or a dense core after a supernova) and scatters material that seeds new stars — death is not total disappearance.
The sequencing/matching check confirms recall of the order and branch but does not by itself build the causal mass→fate intuition; use it after hands-on or diagram work.
The awe-imagery and fly-through serve wonder and timescale understanding; they are not required to grasp mass→fate and should not replace the branching model.

The mass dial, lifespan counter, play/rewind controls, Sun preset, tap-to-reveal stages and labelled fork are illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory; any medium that lets a learner vary mass and see the resulting ending and lifespan serves the same purpose.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims are cited as directly supporting the teaching principles (fusion as the shining mechanism; mass deciding death type and lifespan). Citation does not establish that any specific activity here was empirically tested or that one medium is superior to another.

The legacy row asserted '3D adds awe without being needed' and that a quiz/conversation 'can't build the causal intuition' as near-universal claims; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements. Internal fit rankings and artefact-type labels were removed and not treated as pedagogical laws.

Editor note: the summary previously called the interactive 'the richest way' to discover mass→fate; this unqualified superiority claim was softened to 'may be a particularly direct way', consistent with the untested-proposal framing.

Verified-resolved: the earlier branch error (both mass paths routed through a single 'giant', with 'supergiant' only tacked onto the massive path) is corrected so the fork sits at the main sequence with distinct giant (low-mass) and supergiant (high-mass) stages, matching the original key representation across summary, diagram, check and constraints.

Self-audit of science content otherwise found the born→shine→die sequence, fusion of hydrogen to helium, mass-dependent endings, the Sun's white-dwarf fate, and the massive-stars-die-young twist consistent across the pedagogy, assessment and source fields.

probeDeeper: Which lasts longer — a huge massive star or a small one like the Sun — and why is that surprising?
What will actually happen to the Sun at the end of its life, if not a supernova?
What is going on inside a star to make it shine, if it isn't ordinary fire?
What single property of a star decides how it will live and how it will die?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the Sun is too small to explode as a supernova. At the end of its life it will swell into a red giant, then gently shed its outer layers and shrink into a white dwarf; only much more massive stars end in supernovae. And the puzzle's answer is surprising: the biggest, most massive stars actually live the SHORTEST lives, not the longest. Even though they hold more fuel, they burn it enormously faster and more furiously, so they last only a few million years, while a small star like the Sun sips its fuel and shines for billions of years. A star's MASS decides both how it lives and how it dies.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Only much more massive stars supernova; the Sun will become a red giant and then a white dwarf — no explosion.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Stars shine by nuclear FUSION — joining hydrogen into helium in the core — not by ordinary burning; there's no fire and no oxygen out there.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks big stars live longest and/or the Sun will supernova; may believe stars burn like fire.
responseLevels.full: Explains mass decides fate and lifespan — massive stars burn fast and die young in supernovae, small stars like the Sun last billions of years and end as white dwarfs — and that stars shine by fusion, not burning.
responseLevels.partial: Describes the stages (nebula → fusion → death) and knows massive stars supernova, but holds the more-fuel-longer-life idea or is unsure of the Sun's fate.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Our Sun is a fairly small-to-medium star. When it reaches the end of its life, will it explode in a giant supernova like the biggest stars do? And here's a puzzle: do the biggest, most massive stars live the LONGEST, because they have the most fuel? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two intuitive-but-wrong ideas are tested at once: that the Sun will supernova, and that more fuel means a longer life. A child who understands stellar life cycles says the Sun becomes a white dwarf (no supernova) and that massive stars die fastest because they burn fuel far faster. The 'why' tier surfaces the mass-decides-fate-and-lifespan idea.
